column1: # The protected set — the machine-readable rendering of schema/PROTECTED.md.
# schema/PROTECTED.md is the authority. This file is what src/prune.ts reads, and
# test/prune.test.ts fails if anything named in that document is missing here.
# Nothing in this file can be named by a recipe: prune.also_remove takes values from a closed list
# and none of these appears on it. This file is the SECOND layer — the one that holds when the
# removal closure, which is not a well-behaved function, tries to take one of them as a dependency.
#   role      which link of the repair chain this is
#   why       the sentence printed when a plan would remove it

column3: why
bootc is the thing that swaps one whole operating system for the next one on restart. Without it this fleet receives no repair ever again.
rpm-ostree is how a bootc image is staged and committed. Removing it strands the machine on the image it has.
ostree stores the deployments. Removing it removes both the running system and the one it would roll back to.
bootupd updates the bootloader. A machine whose bootloader can never be updated is a machine that will one day not boot.

greenboot is the thing that checks the machine reached a login screen after an update and puts the old one back if it did not. Removing it converts a bad update from an inconvenience into a site visit.
The health checks greenboot runs. Keeping greenboot and removing its checks gives you a safety net that always reports success.
The bootloader. greenboot's rollback counts boot attempts through it (D9), so this is part of the safety net and not merely part of starting up.
The signed first-stage loader. Removing it makes the image unbootable on every Secure Boot machine, which is most of them.
systemd is the thing that starts everything else on this list.
Without udev there is no disk, no network card and no keyboard.
The message bus every desktop and system service talks over.
NetworkManager is the thing that reaches the network. Every repair this machine will ever receive arrives through it.
The authorisation layer the policy modes are enforced through. Removing it does not make the machine more open, it makes the policy unprovable.
The confinement the image is hardened with. An image that reports a policy it is not running is worse than one that reports none.
Required for the signature policy and the image store to work under SELinux.
Carries /etc/containers/policy.json — the rule that says an image we did not sign does not get installed (D8).
Used by the update agent to inspect and verify what it is about to install.
Removing the package manager is the classic way a prune makes an image impossible to build on or repair.
The package database itself. Without it nothing can report what is installed, including the removal report.
A screen reader. We do not sell an image a blind pupil cannot use, in any policy mode, at any price.
A screen magnifier. Same rule.
An on-screen keyboard. Same rule.
An on-screen keyboard. Same rule.
The speech engine the screen reader talks through. Keeping the reader and removing its voice is a reader that says nothing.
The kernel belongs to the base image. A recipe cannot name it at all; this row is what stops a closure taking it.
